title: Valid Palindrome
problemStatement: Given a string s, return true if it is a palindrome after converting all uppercase letters to lowercase and removing all non-alphanumeric characters.

examples.input: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"

constraints: s consists of printable ASCII characters
approachSteps: A palindrome reads the same forward and backward — you want to compare characters from both ends moving inward.
Use two pointers, one starting at the left end and one at the right end.
Skip any character that isn't alphanumeric by advancing the relevant pointer, without comparing it.
When both pointers point at alphanumeric characters, compare them case-insensitively; if they differ, it's not a palindrome.
Move both pointers inward and repeat until they meet or cross.

bruteForce.approach: Build a cleaned, lowercased copy of the string, then compare it to its reverse.

optimalApproach: Two pointers moving inward from both ends, skipping non-alphanumeric characters in place, avoids building a second string.
timeComplexity: O(n) — each character is visited at most once by either pointer.
spaceComplexity: O(1) extra space — no copy of the string is built.
followUps: How would you solve 'Valid Palindrome II' where you may delete at most one character?
Does this approach work as-is for Unicode letters, or does .isalnum()/.lower() need care there?

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problemStatement: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
approachSteps: The brute force checks every substring for uniqueness, which re-examines overlapping characters repeatedly — look for a way to reuse work as the window slides.
Maintain a window [left, right] that always contains only unique characters, and grow right one step at a time.
Track the last-seen index of each character in a hash map so you can jump left directly instead of shrinking one step at a time.
When you see a character already in the window (its last-seen index >= left), move left to just past that previous occurrence.
After each step, update the best (longest) window length seen so far.

bruteForce.approach: Check every substring for repeated characters.
bruteForce.timeComplexity: O(n^3) or O(n^2) with a running set

optimalApproach: Sliding window with a hash map of last-seen index per character; left jumps directly to avoid rescanning, so each character is processed a constant number of times.
timeComplexity: O(n) — right advances once per character; left only ever moves forward, never resets, across the whole scan.
spaceComplexity: O(min(n, alphabet size)) for the last-seen map.
followUps: How would you adapt this to find the longest substring with at most k distinct characters?
What breaks if you shrink left one step at a time instead of jumping — does the complexity change?

title: Minimum Window Substring
problemStatement: Given two strings s and t, return the minimum window substring of s such that every character in t (including duplicates) is included in the window. Return an empty string if no such window exists.
approachSteps: You need a window over s that contains at least the required count of every character in t — track 'what's still needed' rather than re-checking full counts each time.
Build a frequency map of t, and track how many distinct required characters are currently 'satisfied' in the current window.
Expand the window by moving right forward, decrementing the needed count for that character, and marking it satisfied once its count reaches zero.
Once all required characters are satisfied, try to shrink from left as much as possible while it stays valid — every valid window is a candidate for the answer.
Each time you shrink past a required character, that character becomes unsatisfied again, and you resume expanding right.
Track the smallest valid window's start and length throughout.

bruteForce.approach: Check every substring of s against t's character requirements.

optimalApproach: Sliding window with two pointers and a 'need vs have' counter: expand right to satisfy requirements, then greedily contract left while still valid, recording the smallest valid window.
timeComplexity: O(n + m) where n = len(s), m = len(t) — left and right each traverse s at most once.
spaceComplexity: O(m) for the character-count map (bounded by the alphabet of t).
followUps: Why is tracking a single 'missing' counter better than comparing full frequency maps on every step?
How would you return all minimal windows instead of just one?

title: Find All Anagrams in a String
problemStatement: Given two strings s and p, return an array of all the start indices of p's anagrams in s. You may return the answer in any order.

examples.explanation: Substrings starting at index 0 ("cba") and index 6 ("bac") are anagrams of "abc".

approachSteps: Unlike the general 'longest substring' sliding window, this window has a FIXED size (len(p)) — that simplifies things, since you always shrink by exactly one whenever you grow by one.
Track a frequency count of what the window currently needs (need) versus what characters have reached their required count in the current window (a 'formed' counter).
As you extend the window's right edge, increment that character's count, and increment formed if it just reached exactly the needed count for that character.

Once the window exceeds length len(p), shrink from the left the same way in reverse — decrementing formed first if removing that character drops it below the needed count, then decrementing its window count.
Whenever the window is exactly length len(p) AND formed equals the total number of distinct required characters, the window's start index is a valid anagram match.

bruteForce.approach: For every window of length len(p) in s, build a fresh character count (or sort the substring) and compare it against p's character count.
bruteForce.timeComplexity: O(n * k) or O(n * k log k) with sorting, where k = len(p)

optimalApproach: Fixed-size sliding window tracking a 'formed vs required' counter so each window transition is O(1), instead of recomputing/comparing a full frequency map at every position.
timeComplexity: O(n) — each character enters and leaves the window at most once; the formed counter update is O(1) per step.
spaceComplexity: O(k) for the need/window frequency maps, bounded by the alphabet of p.
followUps: How does this problem's fixed-size window differ from Minimum Window Substring's variable-size window — why does that make this one simpler?
How would you adapt this to find the FIRST anagram match only, and stop early once found?

title: Valid Triangle Number
problemStatement: Given an integer array nums, return the number of triplets chosen from the array that can make the sides of a triangle (i.e. satisfy the triangle inequality: the sum of any two sides must exceed the third).
approachSteps: The brute force checks all O(n^3) triplets — but if you sort first, you only need ONE inequality check per triplet (a + b > c, where c is the largest), since the others (a + c > b, b + c > a) are automatically true when a <= b <= c.
Sort the array ascending, then fix the LARGEST side of the triangle at index k, scanning k from the end of the array down to index 2.
For a fixed k, use two pointers i (from the start) and j (from k-1) scanning inward: if nums[i] + nums[j] > nums[k], the triangle inequality holds for this pair with the largest side.

Here's the key shortcut: if nums[i] + nums[j] > nums[k] holds, then it ALSO holds for every index between i and j-1 paired with j (since the array is sorted, those values are all >= nums[i]) — so you can count all of them at once (j - i) rather than checking one by one, then shrink j.
If nums[i] + nums[j] <= nums[k], no pairing with this i can work with this j either (i is the smallest possible contributor), so advance i instead.

bruteForce.approach: Check every triplet of indices (i, j, k) and test the triangle inequality directly.

optimalApproach: Sort the array, then for each fixed largest side, use two pointers scanning inward — counting multiple valid pairs at once instead of checking each individually.
timeComplexity: O(n^2) — sorting is O(n log n), and for each of the n choices of k, the two-pointer scan is O(n), giving O(n^2) total.
spaceComplexity: O(1) extra (excluding the space used by the sort itself).
followUps: Walk through why 'count += j - i' is valid — why does the sortedness guarantee ALL of those intermediate pairs also satisfy the inequality?
How would you adapt this two-pointer counting pattern to count triplets satisfying a different inequality, like nums[i] + nums[j] < target (3Sum Smaller)?
